items.passage: As freshwater becomes scarcer, more countries are turning to the sea. Desalination plants remove salt from seawater, producing drinking water for cities that have run out of other sources. The technology is proven: Israel now gets more than half its domestic water from desalination, and large plants operate in Saudi Arabia, Australia and California. The main obstacle is cost. Desalination uses large amounts of energy, and the water it produces is usually more expensive than water from rivers or underground aquifers. A second problem is the brine left behind. For every litre of fresh water, a plant produces about one and a half litres of brine, water twice as salty as the sea, which is usually pumped back into the ocean. If the brine is released too close to shore, it can damage marine life on the seabed. Engineers are working on both problems. Solar-powered plants are being tested in the Middle East, and researchers are finding uses for brine, from extracting minerals to producing salt for industry. Supporters argue that desalination is the only reliable answer for coastal cities facing long droughts. Critics reply that it encourages wasteful use of water, since a city that can make its own water has less reason to fix leaks or use water carefully. The fairest view is that desalination is a valuable backup, but it works best in places that also manage demand, repair pipes, and reuse wastewater.
items.question: Which of the following pairs of statements is BOTH supported by the passage?
options: They are using a valuable backup in the weakest way, since the passage says desalination works best alongside demand management and pipe repair AND the technology is proven and already supplies more than half of Israel's domestic water
They are using a valuable backup in the weakest way, since the passage says desalination works best alongside demand management and pipe repair AND They will no longer need brine disposal
They have solved their water problem, since desalination is the only reliable answer AND the technology is proven and already supplies more than half of Israel's domestic water
It is about twice as salty as seawater and can harm marine life if released close to shore AND They will encourage wasteful use of water in a good way
They have proved that desalination is cheaper than river water AND solar-powered plants have already solved the cost problem
items.explanation: Only the keyed option joins two statements the passage supports: They are using a valuable backup in the weakest way, since the passage says desalination works best alongside demand management and pipe repair and the technology is proven and already supplies more than half of Israel's domestic water. Every other option contains at least one statement the passage does not support: the second half of one option (They will no longer need brine disposal); the first half of another (They have solved their water problem, since desalination is the only reliable answer); the second half of a third (They will encourage wasteful use of water in a good way); and both halves of the last (They have proved that desalination is cheaper than river water and solar-powered plants have already solved the cost problem).

items.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid inference from the passage?
options: A city that builds a desalination plant while also fixing leaks and reusing wastewater is following the fairest view the passage offers.
The brine problem and the energy problem are presented as separate obstacles, so solving one would still leave the other to be addressed.
Critics would likely say that a city which can make its own water may use water less carefully, even if the plant itself runs on solar power.
Because desalination is proven and supplies more than half of Israel's water, the author believes every coastal city should build a plant and stop repairing leaks.
Desalination may be the only reliable answer for a coastal city in a long drought, yet still be too expensive for everyday use without cheaper energy.
items.explanation: Options A, B, C and E all follow from the passage: the fairest view is that desalination is a valuable backup that works best in places that also manage demand, repair pipes and reuse wastewater; the main obstacle is cost and energy while brine is presented as a second problem; critics reply that a city which can make its own water has less reason to fix leaks or use water carefully, and solar power addresses the energy problem rather than that incentive; and supporters call desalination the only reliable answer for coastal cities facing long droughts while the water it produces is usually more expensive than water from rivers or aquifers. Only option D is not valid: the passage says desalination works best alongside pipe repair and demand management, so proven technology is not a reason to stop repairing leaks.

items.question: A coastal city builds a desalination plant, powers it with solar energy, and at the same time fixes its leaks and reuses wastewater. What would the author most likely say?
options: It proves desalination is cheaper than river water.
It encourages wasteful use, since the passage says any desalination does so.

It is using desalination in the way the passage calls fairest: as a valuable backup alongside demand management, while the solar power addresses the cost problem the passage names as the main obstacle.
It has solved the brine problem, since solar power removes the brine.
It is wasting money, since the passage says desalination never works.
items.explanation: The fairest view in the passage is that desalination is a valuable backup, but it works best in places that also manage demand, repair pipes and reuse wastewater. The main obstacle is cost, because desalination uses large amounts of energy, and solar-powered plants are being tested. The critics' charge that it encourages wasteful use applies to cities that do not manage demand.

items.question: Which statement best captures the relationship between the supporters' and the critics' arguments about desalination, as the passage presents them?
options: Both sides agree desalination is cheaper than river water.
The critics say brine is harmless, and the supporters say it is the main problem.
The passage says the two sides agree on everything.

The supporters call it the only reliable answer for drought-hit coastal cities; the critics reply that it encourages wasteful use, since a city that can make its own water has less reason to fix leaks or use water carefully.
The supporters say desalination is unproven, and the critics say it is the only answer.
items.explanation: Supporters argue desalination is the only reliable answer for coastal cities facing long droughts. Critics reply that it encourages wasteful use of water, since a city that can make its own water has less reason to fix leaks or use water carefully. The passage presents both positions before giving its own fairest view.

items.passage: For decades, night trains across Europe were in decline. Budget airlines offered cheaper and faster journeys, and railway companies found sleeper carriages expensive to run. By 2016, several countries had cancelled their last overnight services. Then the trend reversed. A new generation of travellers, concerned about the carbon emissions of flying, began to look for alternatives, and the night train offered something a plane could not: a bed, a slow journey through the landscape, and arrival in the city centre in the morning. The Austrian railway company led the revival, expanding its Nightjet network to connect Vienna with cities such as Amsterdam, Rome and Paris. Other operators followed, and new routes are now announced almost every year. The economics remain difficult. A sleeper train carries fewer passengers than a daytime train, and the carriages need staff through the night. Ticket prices are often higher than a budget flight, though supporters point out that the fare includes a night of accommodation. The revival also depends on infrastructure: border crossings, track maintenance and the availability of sleeper carriages all limit how fast the network can grow. Even so, the return of the night train shows how quickly a transport habit can change when travellers weigh comfort and climate alongside price, and when a railway company is willing to invest in a service that had been written off.
items.question: Which of the following pairs of statements is BOTH supported by the passage?
options: It may be higher than a budget flight, but supporters argue it includes a night of accommodation AND That budget airlines have stopped flying in Europe
That border crossings no longer limit rail travel AND They are difficult because sleeper trains carry fewer passengers and need night staff
show which company led the revival of night trains AND That ticket prices are always lower than budget flights
That sleeper trains are cheaper to run than daytime trains AND It is set by the Austrian railway company for all of Europe
It may be higher than a budget flight, but supporters argue it includes a night of accommodation AND They are difficult because sleeper trains carry fewer passengers and need night staff
items.explanation: Only the keyed option joins two statements the passage supports: It may be higher than a budget flight, but supporters argue it includes a night of accommodation and They are difficult because sleeper trains carry fewer passengers and need night staff. Every other option contains at least one statement the passage does not support: the second half of one option (That budget airlines have stopped flying in Europe); the first half of another (That border crossings no longer limit rail travel); the second half of a third (That ticket prices are always lower than budget flights); and both halves of the last (That sleeper trains are cheaper to run than daytime trains and It is set by the Austrian railway company for all of Europe).

items.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid inference from the passage?
options: Because sleeper carriages need staff through the night and carry fewer passengers, the economics of night trains remain difficult even as the network grows.
Because travellers began to weigh comfort and climate alongside price, a slower journey with a bed could win back passengers who had chosen budget flights.
Because ticket prices are often higher than a budget flight, the revival must be driven by price alone, and comfort and climate play no part in it.
Because the Austrian railway led the revival by expanding its Nightjet network, one company willing to invest in a written-off service can start a wider return.
Because the fare includes a night of accommodation, supporters can argue that a ticket dearer than a budget flight is not dearer than flight plus hotel.
items.explanation: Options A, B, D and E all follow from the passage: fewer passengers plus night staff make the economics difficult; comfort and climate alongside price explain why travellers returned to a slower journey with a bed; the Austrian expansion shows one investing company starting the wider revival; and the included night of accommodation is the supporters' answer to the higher ticket price. Only option C is not valid: it inverts the author's point, which is that the habit changed precisely because travellers weighed comfort and climate alongside price, not because price alone drove the revival.

items.question: A railway launches a night train with cheap fares but no beds, arguing that price alone will fill it. What would the author most likely say?
options: It is the model the Austrian company used.
It misses what the passage says drove the revival: travellers weighed comfort and climate alongside price, and the bed and the slow journey were part of what a plane could not offer.
It follows the passage, since the passage says price is all travellers weigh.
It will succeed because the passage says night trains are cheap to run.
It proves the revival was caused by budget airlines stopping flights.
items.explanation: The revival came when travellers concerned about carbon emissions looked for alternatives, and the night train offered something a plane could not: a bed, a slow journey through the landscape, and arrival in the city centre in the morning. The passage says the habit changed when travellers weighed comfort and climate alongside price.

items.question: Which statement best captures the relationship between the revival of night trains and their economics, as the passage presents it?
options: The revival failed because no one would pay the higher fares.
The passage says infrastructure no longer limits the network.

The revival is real, driven by climate concern and comfort, but the economics remain difficult, since sleeper trains carry fewer passengers, need night staff, and often cost more than a budget flight.
The revival happened because night trains became cheaper to run than daytime trains.
The economics are easy, since ticket prices are always lower than flights.
items.explanation: The trend reversed as a new generation of travellers looked for alternatives to flying, and the Austrian railway led the revival. But the economics remain difficult: a sleeper train carries fewer passengers than a daytime train, the carriages need staff through the night, and ticket prices are often higher than a budget flight. Border crossings, track maintenance and carriage availability still limit growth.

items.passage: In a concrete building on a Norwegian island, more than a million seed samples sit in frozen vaults. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault was built to protect the world's crop diversity against war, disaster and climate change. If a seed bank in a war zone is destroyed, or a crop variety is lost to drought, copies stored in Svalbard can be used to rebuild it. The idea is simple, but its importance is growing. Modern farming relies on a small number of high-yielding varieties, and thousands of traditional varieties have already disappeared. Those lost varieties may carry genes for drought resistance, disease resistance, or tolerance to salty soil, traits that could become vital as the climate changes. Critics of the vault argue that storing seeds is not enough. Seeds in a vault do not evolve with changing pests and diseases, while seeds grown by farmers adapt each season. Supporters reply that the vault is a backup, not a replacement for farming. Its purpose is to ensure that no variety is lost forever, so that breeders and farmers can draw on it when they need a trait that has vanished from the fields. The vault has already been used: seeds stored there were withdrawn to rebuild a seed bank in Lebanon after the original collection in Syria was damaged by war. The lesson is that diversity is a form of insurance, and insurance is worth little if it is bought only after the disaster.
items.question: Which of the following pairs of statements is BOTH supported by the passage?
options: It would guarantee that no variety is ever lost AND show that the vault has already proved useful in practice
It would lose the adaptation that comes from seeds grown by farmers each season, since vault seeds do not evolve with pests and diseases AND It would prove the critics of the vault wrong
insurance should be bought only after a disaster has happened AND modern farming should use more varieties at once
Static conservation preserves a variety as it was, but it cannot preserve the process by which varieties keep adapting AND show that the vault has already proved useful in practice
Static conservation preserves a variety as it was, but it cannot preserve the process by which varieties keep adapting AND It would make the vault unnecessary, since field seeds adapt faster
items.explanation: Only the keyed option joins two statements the passage supports: Static conservation preserves a variety as it was, but it cannot preserve the process by which varieties keep adapting and show that the vault has already proved useful in practice. Every other option contains at least one statement the passage does not support: the second half of one option (It would make the vault unnecessary, since field seeds adapt faster); the first half of another (It would guarantee that no variety is ever lost); the second half of a third (It would prove the critics of the vault wrong); and both halves of the last (insurance should be bought only after a disaster has happened and modern farming should use more varieties at once).

items.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid inference from the passage?
options: Because vault seeds do not evolve with pests and diseases while farm-grown seeds adapt each season, static conservation preserves a variety as it was but not the process of adaptation.
Because the vault is a backup and not a replacement for farming, protecting varieties before they are lost is worthwhile even though the benefit is not immediate.
Because seeds stored in Svalbard were withdrawn to rebuild a seed bank in Lebanon after the Syrian collection was damaged by war, the vault has already proved useful in practice.
Because vault seeds do not evolve, the vault should replace farming entirely, and farmers need not grow traditional varieties any more.

Because modern farming relies on a small number of high-yielding varieties while thousands of traditional ones have disappeared, the lost varieties may carry traits that become vital as the climate changes.
items.explanation: Options A, B, C and E all follow from the passage: vault seeds do not evolve while farm seeds adapt, so static conservation cannot preserve the process; the vault as a backup justifies protecting varieties before they are lost; the Lebanon withdrawal shows the vault already used in practice; and reliance on few high-yielding varieties makes lost traits potentially vital. Only option D is not valid: it inverts the passage's explicit point, which is that the vault is a backup, not a replacement for farming, and supporters reply to critics on exactly that ground.

items.question: Two countries act on the passage's argument. Country X stores all its varieties in a vault and stops growing traditional varieties in its fields. Country Y keeps growing traditional varieties in its fields and also stores copies in a vault. What would the author most likely say?
options: Neither follows the author's view, because the passage opposes all seed vaults.
X follows the author's view and Y wastes effort, because field growing adds nothing the vault cannot provide.
X follows the author's view and Y does not, because the vault alone preserves everything.
Y follows the author's view and X misunderstands it: the vault is a backup, not a replacement, and vault seeds do not evolve with pests and diseases as field-grown seeds do.
Both follow the author's view, because the passage treats vault storage and field growing as interchangeable.
items.explanation: The passage says supporters reply that the vault is a backup, not a replacement for farming, and it reports the critics' point that seeds in a vault do not evolve with changing pests and diseases while seeds grown by farmers adapt each season. Country Y does exactly what the passage endorses, keeping field growing and using the vault as a backup. Country X does the opposite, treating the vault as a replacement, which misunderstands its purpose. Options C, E and B all claim the vault alone is enough, which the passage denies. Option A is wrong because the passage supports the vault as a backup.

items.question: Which statement best captures the relationship between static conservation in the vault and growing seeds in fields, as the passage presents it?
options: The passage says vault seeds decay within a few years.
The vault preserves a variety as it was, so it can be drawn on when a trait is needed; field growing preserves the process by which varieties keep adapting to pests and diseases.
Both preserve exactly the same thing, so the critics' objection is groundless.
Field growing preserves nothing, since farmers lose varieties every season.
The vault preserves adaptation, while fields preserve only the variety as it was.
items.explanation: The critics' argument is that static conservation preserves a variety as it was, but it cannot preserve the process by which varieties keep adapting. Seeds in a vault do not evolve with changing pests and diseases, while seeds grown by farmers adapt each season. The vault's purpose is to ensure no variety is lost forever.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) Yet for all its centuries of service, the windmill had a weakness: dependence on the weather, so on a calm day the mill stood still. (B) This simple mechanism ground grain for centuries before steam power arrived. (C) The windmill's sails turn a shaft that drives the millstones below. (D) Millers answered this weakness by building towers that could turn to face the wind. (E) A miller who could turn his tower into the wind could grind on days when his neighbours' mills stood still.
items.explanation: The correct order is CBADE. The order is forced by these links: 'This simple mechanism' in B needs the sails and shaft in C; 'its centuries of service' in A needs the centuries in B; 'this weakness' in D needs the weather dependence in A; 'turn his tower' and 'mills stood still' in E need the towers in D and the still mill in A. Every other order breaks at least one of them: a sentence that refers back to something not yet mentioned, or that belongs to a case not yet stated, cannot come earlier.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) That luxury trade ended only when factory-made ice became cheaper than ice cut from a lake. (B) The stored blocks were packed in sawdust, which slowed melting through the summer. (C) This trade made ice a luxury in warm cities, where a block could sell for many times its cost. (D) Before refrigeration, ice was cut from frozen lakes in winter and stored in insulated houses. (E) When factory ice finally became cheaper, the lake trade ended, but the sawdust trade it had created carried on for years.
items.explanation: The correct order is DBCAE. The order is forced by these links: 'The stored blocks' in B need the cut and stored ice in D; 'This trade' in C needs the storage and sale in B; 'That luxury trade' in A needs the luxury trade in C, and 'ice cut from a lake' needs D; 'When factory ice finally became cheaper' in E needs the cheaper factory ice in A. Every other order breaks at least one of them: a sentence that refers back to something not yet mentioned, or that belongs to a case not yet stated, cannot come earlier.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) Semaphore towers relayed messages across France by moving wooden arms into coded positions. (B) This speed mattered to the army, which used the towers to send orders faster than any rider. (C) The system faded once the electric telegraph could send the same message without line of sight. (D) Each tower was placed within sight of the next, so a signal could travel hundreds of kilometres in an hour. (E) The army's orders travelled this way, tower to tower, and an operator who missed a signal had to ask the previous tower to repeat it while the whole line waited.
items.explanation: The correct order is ADBEC. The order is forced by these links: 'the next' in D needs the towers in A; 'This speed' in B needs the hour-long journey in D; C is the end of the system the army used in B; 'the previous tower' in E needs the towers in D; 'The army's orders' in E need the army's use of the towers in B; E describes operating the system while it lived, before it faded in C. Every other order breaks at least one of them: a sentence that refers back to something not yet mentioned, or that belongs to a case not yet stated, cannot come earlier.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) Each night he climbed the tower to light the lamp that guided ships away from the rocks. (B) In storms, he stayed awake to keep the light burning through the night. (C) A lighthouse keeper's job was lonely but vital. (D) Today, most lighthouses are automated, but the towers still stand as reminders of that work. (E) Like the towers, the keepers' logbooks, filled with notes on storms and passing ships, are now kept in museums as records of a vanished way of life. What is the correct order?
items.explanation: The correct order is CABDE. The order is forced by these links: 'he' in A is the keeper in C; 'he' in B continues the nightly duty in A; 'Today' in D contrasts with the past job in A and B; 'Like the towers' in E needs the towers in D. Every other order breaks at least one of them: a sentence that refers back to something not yet mentioned, or that belongs to a case not yet stated, cannot come earlier.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) The boat enters the chamber, the gates close, and water is let in or out until the levels match. (B) A canal lock lifts a boat between two stretches of water at different heights. (C) This slow rise or fall is the price of travelling on a canal instead of a river. (D) Modern boats still use locks built two centuries ago, because that slow rise and fall has never needed a better method. (E) That unchanged principle is simple enough that a child can work a lock after watching once, yet it has lifted boats over hills that no river could climb.
items.explanation: The correct order is BACDE. The order is forced by these links: 'the chamber' and 'the levels' in A need the lock introduced in B; 'This slow rise or fall' in C needs the water let in or out in A; 'that slow rise and fall' in D needs the rise or fall named in C; 'That unchanged principle' in E needs the method that 'has never needed a better method' in D. Every other order breaks at least one of them: the distractor BACED now fails because E comes before D, so 'That unchanged principle' has no antecedent, since nothing before it has been described as unchanged.

items.question: Which pair bears the same relation as Filter : Water, where the first removes impurities from the second, and the removal happens as the second passes through the first?
items.explanation: A sieve removes lumps and impurities from flour as the flour passes through it, which matches both halves of the relation: removal of impurities and passage through the first object. An oven transforms bread rather than removing impurities from it. A knife cuts bread without anything passing through it. A bottle contains water without removing anything. A kettle heats water without removing impurities.

items.question: Which pair bears the same relation as Cure : Disease, and also meets this condition: the first term removes the second entirely, rather than merely managing it?
items.explanation: The relation is remedy to the affliction it resolves, and the remedy must remove the affliction entirely. A cure removes a disease, as a solution removes a problem. A treatment manages an illness but does not necessarily remove it. The reversed pair breaks the relation, and the other options are agent to recipient and thing to place.

items.question: Which pair bears the same relation as Flood : Damage, and also meets this condition: the effect is a harmful condition suffered by people, not merely another natural event?
items.explanation: The relation is cause to effect, and the effect must be a harmful condition suffered by people. A flood causes damage, as a drought causes scarcity. Rain causes a flood, but a flood is another natural event, not itself a harmful condition suffered by people. The reversed pair breaks the causal direction, and the other options are part to whole and agent to recipient.

items.question: Which pair bears the same relation as Sculptor : Statue, and also meets this condition: the creation is presented to an audience, rather than read alone?
items.explanation: The relation is creator to creation, and the creation must be presented to an audience. A statue is viewed by visitors, as a play is performed for an audience. A novel is read alone by its reader, not presented to an audience. The reversed pair breaks the relation, and the other options are agent to instrument and whole to part.

items.question: Which pair bears the same relation as Famine : Relief, and also meets this condition: the response is an action or a payment, not a physical substance?
items.explanation: The relation is affliction to the response that removes it, and the response must be an action or a payment. Relief is aid given to end a famine, as repayment is a payment that ends a debt. Medicine is a physical substance used to treat an illness, not an action or a payment. The reversed pair breaks the relation, and the other options are instrument to action and part to whole.

items.question: Choose the pair in which the first word best fits the blank and the second word is its closest synonym. His reading was ___, jumping from astronomy to cookery to law without ever finishing a subject.
items.explanation: Only the pair 'desultory - random' meets both conditions: the first word fits the blank, and the second word is its closest synonym. The trap is 'systematic - random': random does fit the blank, but systematic does not mean random (systematic means methodical), so that pair fails the synonym condition. Desultory means random and disconnected. Systematic is its opposite, assiduous and relentless describe sustained effort, and profound describes depth, not order.

items.question: Choose the pair in which the first word best fits the blank and the second word is its closest synonym. Her reply was ___, cutting straight to the flaw in the argument and leaving the committee with nothing to say.
items.explanation: Only the pair 'trenchant - incisive' meets both conditions: the first word fits the blank, and the second word is its closest synonym. The trap is 'rambling - incisive': incisive does fit the blank, but rambling does not mean incisive (rambling means discursive), so that pair fails the synonym condition. Trenchant means sharp and incisive. Rambling and vague are its opposite, hesitant weakens it, and obsequious describes flattery, not sharpness.

items.question: Choose the pair in which the first word best fits the blank and the second word is its closest synonym. The scandal brought ___ on the whole department, and its reputation took years to recover.
items.explanation: Only the pair 'opprobrium - disgrace' meets both conditions: the first word fits the blank, and the second word is its closest synonym. The trap is 'acclaim - disgrace': disgrace does fit the blank, but acclaim does not mean disgrace (acclaim means praise), so that pair fails the synonym condition. Opprobrium means public disgrace. Acclaim is its opposite, indifference and sympathy are other reactions, and notoriety, though it fits the blank, is paired with honour, which is its opposite, not its synonym.

items.question: Choose the pair in which the first word best fits the blank and the second word is its closest synonym. The old clerk was ___ in his habits, doing the same tasks in the same order every morning for thirty years.
items.explanation: Only the pair 'methodical - systematic' meets both conditions: the first word fits the blank, and the second word is its closest synonym. The trap is 'erratic - systematic': systematic does fit the blank, but erratic does not mean systematic (erratic means unpredictable), so that pair fails the synonym condition. Methodical means orderly and systematic. Erratic, impetuous and desultory are its opposites, and reluctant describes willingness, not order.

items.question: Choose the pair in which the first word best fits the blank and the second word is its closest synonym. The committee's ___ report, which praised everyone and criticised no one, left the members unsure what, if anything, needed to change.
items.explanation: Anodyne means inoffensive and deliberately unlikely to cause offence, which fits a report that praised everyone and criticised no one, and its closest synonym here is bland. Candid and trenchant both imply sharp honesty, which contradicts a report that criticised no one. Scathing is the opposite of the report described. In option E the first word fits but harsh is an antonym of anodyne, not a synonym.

items.question: Which TWO parts of the sentence below contain errors? Whom did you say is coming to the meeting, and to who should I address the invitation?
options: "Whom did you say" and "and to who should I address"
"Whom did you say" and "is coming to the meeting"
"is coming to the meeting" and "and to who should I address"
"and to who should I address" and "the invitation"
items.explanation: Two errors, and they are mirror images of one rule: 'who' is the subject form and 'whom' is the object form, and this sentence swaps them in both halves. 'Whom did you say is coming' is wrong because the word is the subject of 'is', so the sentence needs 'Who did you say is coming'. 'To who should I address the invitation' is wrong because the word is the object of the preposition 'to', so the sentence needs 'to whom should I address the invitation'. A solver who corrects both halves in the same direction, using 'who' twice or 'whom' twice, still leaves one error behind. 'Is coming to the meeting' and 'the invitation' are both correct.

items.question: Which TWO parts of the sentence below contain errors? The furniture in the three rooms were damaged in transit, and the supplier has agreed to replace them.
options: "were damaged in transit" and "to replace them"
"The furniture in the three rooms" and "to replace them"
"were damaged in transit" and "and the supplier has agreed"
"The furniture in the three rooms" and "were damaged in transit"
"and the supplier has agreed" and "to replace them"
items.explanation: Two errors, and they turn on the same fact: furniture is a singular uncountable noun, so both the verb and the pronoun that refer to it must be singular. Were damaged is wrong: the subject is furniture, singular, so the verb must be was damaged. To replace them is wrong: them is plural, so the pronoun must be it. The trap is the three rooms, a plural phrase sitting between the subject and the verb that tempts the solver to use a plural verb. The furniture in the three rooms and the supplier has agreed are both correct.

items.question: Which TWO parts of the sentence below contain errors? She is the most intelligent of the two sisters, and he is the more intelligent of the three brothers.
options: "She is the most intelligent" and "and he is the more intelligent"
"She is the most intelligent" and "of the two sisters"
"of the two sisters" and "and he is the more intelligent"
"She is the most intelligent" and "of the three brothers"
"and he is the more intelligent" and "of the three brothers"
items.explanation: Two errors, and they are mirror images of one rule: the comparative is used for two things and the superlative for three or more, and this sentence swaps them in both halves. 'The most intelligent of the two sisters' is wrong: with two sisters the sentence needs the comparative, 'the more intelligent'. 'The more intelligent of the three brothers' is wrong: with three brothers the sentence needs the superlative, 'the most intelligent'. A solver who corrects both halves in the same direction, using the comparative twice or the superlative twice, still leaves one error behind. 'Of the two sisters' and 'of the three brothers' are both correct.

items.question: Which TWO parts of the sentence below contain errors? She did not hardly sleep last night, and he could not scarcely hear the announcement.
options: "did not hardly sleep" and "could not scarcely hear"
items.explanation: Two errors, and they are mirror images of one rule: hardly and scarcely are already negative, so they must not be combined with not, and this sentence does it in both halves. Did not hardly sleep is wrong: not and hardly are both negatives, so the sentence needs she hardly slept. Could not scarcely hear is wrong for the same reason: the sentence needs he could scarcely hear. A solver who removes only one not still leaves a double negative behind. Last night is correct, and the subjects she and he are correct.

items.question: Which TWO parts of the sentence below contain errors? Either the manager or the workers has the keys, and neither of them have informed security.
options: "Either the manager or the workers" and "has the keys"
"Either the manager or the workers" and "have informed security"
"has the keys" and "and neither of them"
"and neither of them" and "have informed security"
items.explanation: Two errors, and they turn on one rule applied in opposite directions. With 'either ... or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, so 'Either the manager or the workers has the keys' is wrong: the nearer subject is 'the workers', plural, so the verb must be 'have the keys'. With 'neither', the word itself is singular, so 'neither of them have informed security' is wrong: the verb must be 'has informed security'. One verb must go plural and the other singular, so a solver who makes both verbs agree the same way still leaves one error behind. The two subject phrases themselves are both correct.

items.question: Which TWO parts of the sentence below contain errors? The number of students who have applied have increased, and each of them have submitted the form on time.
options: "The number of students" and "who have applied"
"have increased" and "and each of them have submitted the form on time"
"who have applied" and "and each of them have submitted the form on time"
items.explanation: Two errors, and both turn on the same trap: the verb must agree with its real subject, not with the nearest plural noun. 'The number of students ... have increased' is wrong: the subject is 'the number', singular, so the verb must be 'has increased'. 'Each of them have submitted' is wrong: 'each' is singular, so the verb must be 'has submitted'. The tempting part is 'who have applied', which looks wrong under the same nearest-noun rule but is correct: 'who' refers to 'students', which is plural, so 'have' is right. A solver who applies agreement by proximity flags the correct part and misses a real error.

items.question: Which TWO parts of the sentence below contain errors? She is more intelligent than any student in the class, and her sister, who is two years older, is more intelligent than her.
options: "She is more intelligent than any student" and "than her"
"She is more intelligent than any student" and "in the class"
"She is more intelligent than any student" and "and her sister, who is two years older, is more intelligent"
"and her sister, who is two years older, is more intelligent" and "than her"
items.explanation: Two errors, and both turn on completing an elliptical comparison correctly. 'More intelligent than any student in the class' is wrong: she is herself a student in the class, so the comparison would include her, and the sentence needs 'than any other student'. 'More intelligent than her' is wrong: 'than' here stands for 'than she is', so the subject form is needed and the sentence needs 'than she'. In both halves the obvious reading, comparing her with a group that includes her or with an object form, is the trap. 'In the class' and 'and her sister, who is two years older, is more intelligent' are both correct.

items.question: Which TWO parts of the sentence below contain errors? Whom is responsible for the missing books, and to who should the librarian report the matter?
options: "Whom is responsible" and "for the missing books"
"Whom is responsible" and "and to who should the librarian report"
"for the missing books" and "and to who should the librarian report"
"and to who should the librarian report" and "the matter"
items.explanation: Two errors, and they are mirror images of one rule: 'who' is the subject form and 'whom' is the object form, and this sentence swaps them in both halves. 'Whom is responsible' is wrong because the word is the subject of 'is', so the sentence needs 'Who is responsible'. 'To who should the librarian report' is wrong because the word is the object of the preposition 'to', so the sentence needs 'to whom should the librarian report'. A solver who corrects both halves in the same direction, using 'who' twice or 'whom' twice, still leaves one error behind. 'For the missing books' and 'the matter' are both correct.

items.question: Which TWO parts of the sentence below contain errors? He asked me where was the station, and she asked him when did the train leave.
options: "He asked me" and "when did the train leave"
"and she asked him" and "when did the train leave"
"where was" and "when did the train leave"
items.explanation: Two errors, and they are mirror images of one rule: in reported speech a question takes statement word order, and this sentence keeps question word order in both halves. Where was the station is wrong: in reported speech it must be where the station was. When did the train leave is wrong: it must be when the train left. A solver who corrects only one half still leaves a question-order error behind. He asked me and she asked him are both correct, with ask taking a direct object and no preposition.

items.question: A price is first increased by 20% and then increased by 20%. A second price, starting from the same original value, goes through the same two changes in the opposite order. Which of the following is true?
options: The first ends 4% above the second
Both end 44% above the original price
The second ends 4% above the first
Both end 40% above the original price
The first ends 44% below the original price
items.explanation: Two successive rises of 20% compound: 20 + 20 + 20x20/100 = 44%. The order of the two changes does not matter because the multipliers commute, so both prices end at the same level. Adding the percentages (40%) ignores the increase on the increase, and the order makes no difference of 4%.

items.question: The price of a washing machine is Rs 1,500. Over three seasons it rises by 20%, rises by 10%, falls by 25% in succession. A second machine starts at the same price and goes through the same three changes in reverse order. Which of the following is true?
items.explanation: The three multipliers commute, so the order does not matter: both machines end at Rs 1,500 with the three changes applied in turn, which is Rs 1,485. Applying the summed net percentage 5% to the original price gives Rs 1,575, which is wrong because each change acts on the running price. Neither machine ends Rs 90 higher.

items.question: A shopkeeper buys a mixer, marks it 20% above cost, then gives a discount of 10% on the marked price. The buyer then sells it at a loss of 15% on what he paid, and the second sale takes place for Rs 3,672. What was the shopkeeper's cost price, and what was the marked price? Give the cost price first, then the marked price.
items.explanation: Work backwards from the second sale: the first sale price was Rs 3,672 / 85% = Rs 4,320, the marked price was Rs 4,320 / 90% = Rs 4,800, and the cost was Rs 4,800 / 120% = Rs 4,000. The marked price is 20% above the cost, not above the first sale price, and the discount comes off the marked price, so the cost cannot be read off the second sale price directly.

items.question: A shopkeeper buys a mixer, marks it 20% above cost, then gives a discount of 10% on the marked price. The buyer sells it at a loss of 15%, and the next buyer sells it again at a profit of 25%. The price at the third sale is Rs 4,590. What was the original cost price, and how much more did the third sale fetch than the first sale? Give the cost price first, then the difference.
items.explanation: Work backwards from the third sale: the second sale was Rs 4,590 / 125% = Rs 3,672, the first sale was Rs 3,672 / 85% = Rs 4,320, the marked price was Rs 4,320 / 90% = Rs 4,800, and the cost was Rs 4,800 / 120% = Rs 4,000. The third sale exceeded the first sale by Rs 4,590 - Rs 4,320 = Rs 270. Each percentage acts on a different base, so the chain must be inverted step by step.

items.question: A sum placed at 15% a year on simple interest produces Rs 1,080 of interest. Had the same sum stayed invested for 8 years longer, the interest would have come to Rs 3,240. If the same sum were instead placed at 12% a year, compounded yearly, for 2 years, what total would it grow to?
items.explanation: The interest ratio 3 gives (t+8)/t = 3, so t = 4 years. The principal is Rs 1,080 / (15% x 4) = Rs 1,800. Compounded at 12% for 2 years it becomes Rs 1,800 x 1.2544 = Rs 2257.92. Using the wrong period for the principal, or simple instead of compound interest, gives one of the distractors.

items.question: For a certain sum, the difference between the compound interest and the simple interest for 2 years at 20% a year is Rs 320. What is the difference between the compound interest and the simple interest for 3 years at the same rate, on the same sum?
items.explanation: For 2 years, CI minus SI equals P x (r/100)^2, so P = Rs 320 / 0.04 = Rs 8,000. For 3 years, CI minus SI equals P x ((1 + r/100)^3 - 1 - 3r/100) = Rs 8,000 x 0.1280 = Rs 1,024. The 2-year difference is Rs 320, the 3-year compound interest alone is Rs 5,824, and the 3-year simple interest is Rs 4,800.

items.question: The present ages of two brothers are in the ratio 4:5. In 10 years, their ages will be in the ratio 5:6. What was the ratio of their ages 10 years ago?
items.explanation: Let the ages be 4k and 5k. Then (4k + 10)/(5k + 10) = 5/6 gives k = 10, so the present ages are 40 and 50. 10 years ago they were 30 and 40, a ratio of 3:4. The present ratio 4:5 and the future ratio 5:6 are different questions, and swapping the brothers reverses the ratio.

items.question: A job takes 48 days when 3 weavers, 5 dyers and 4 finishers work on it together, and 20 days when the crew is 6 weavers, 10 dyers and 12 finishers. How long would the same job take a crew of 9 weavers, 15 dyers and 9 finishers?
items.explanation: Let X be the daily work of 3 weavers and 5 dyers together, and let one finishers do c per day. Then X + 4 c = 1/48 and 2X + 12 c = 1/20, giving c = 1/480 and X = 1/80. The target crew does 3X + 9 c = 9/160 of the job per day, so it needs 17 7/9 days. Trying to solve for each worker separately is impossible, and ignoring the finishers in the target crew gives 26 2/3 days.

items.question: A car travels 150 km at 50 km/h and then 150 km at 100 km/h. It then travels 100 km more, and the average speed for the whole journey is 75 km/h. What was its speed on the third leg?
items.explanation: The first two legs take 150/50 = 3 h and 150/100 = 1.50 h. The whole journey is 400 km at 75 km/h, so it takes 400/75 = 5.33 h. The third leg therefore takes 5.33 - 4.50 = 0.83 h, and its speed was 100/0.83 = 120 km/h. The overall average 75 km/h is not the third leg's speed, and the simple mean of the speeds ignores the different times.

items.question: The average age of a group of 8 people is 35 years. One person leaves and a new person joins, and the average becomes 38 years. If instead the new person had joined without anyone leaving, the average of the 9 people would have been 36 years. What are the ages of the departing person and the new person, in that order?
items.explanation: Let the new person's age be y. Joining without a departure gives (8 x 35 + y)/9 = 36, so y = 44. The swap changes the total by y minus the departing age x, and the average rises by 3 over 8 people, so y - x = 24 and x = 20. Swapping the two ages, or using the wrong group size in either step, gives one of the distractors.

items.question: Two positive numbers a and b satisfy ab = 256 and log2 a - log2 b = 2. What is the value of log2(a^3 b^2), and what is a - b? Give the logarithm first, then a - b.
items.explanation: From log2 a - log2 b = 2, a/b = 4, and with ab = 256 this gives a = 32 and b = 8, so log2 a = 5 and log2 b = 3. Then log2(a^3 b^2) = 3 x 5 + 2 x 3 = 21, and a - b = 32 - 8 = 24. Swapping a and b gives the wrong logarithm and a negative difference, and a + b is a different quantity from a - b.

items.question: In an arithmetic progression, the sum of the first 12 terms is 300 and the sum of the first 8 terms is 136. What is the sum of the first 20 terms, and how few terms are needed for the sum to first exceed 1000? Give the sum first, then the number of terms.
items.explanation: From the two sums, 2a + 11d = 50 and 2a + 7d = 34, giving d = 4 and a = 3. The sum of the first 20 terms is 20/2 x (2 x 3 + 19 x 4) = 820. Checking successive partial sums, S_22 = 990 does not exceed 1000, while S_23 = 1081 does, so 23 terms are needed. Scaling a sum directly by the number of terms ignores the changing terms.

items.question: In an arithmetic progression, the sum of the first 12 terms is 300 and the sum of the first 8 terms is 136. What is the 20th term of the progression, and which term is the first to exceed 100? Give the 20th term first, then the term number.
items.explanation: Solving 2a + 11d = 50 and 2a + 7d = 34 gives a = 3 and d = 4, so the 20th term is 3 + 19 x 4 = 79. The 25th term is 99, which does not exceed 100, while the 26th term is 103, the first above 100. An off-by-one in the term index gives one of the distractors.

items.question: What is the smallest integer greater than 200 that leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 5, a remainder of 7 when divided by 11, and a remainder of 2 when divided by 7?
items.explanation: Numbers satisfying the first two conditions are spaced 55 apart, starting at 227. Of those, the first whose remainder on division by 7 is 2 is 282, since 227 leaves remainder 3 on division by 7. The next number satisfying all three is 667, one full least common multiple of 5, 11 and 7 later. A number meeting only two of the three conditions, such as 212 or 205, is not the answer.

items.question: What is the remainder when 9^11 + 4^15 is divided by 7?
items.explanation: Work modulo 7: 9^11 leaves 4 and 4^15 leaves 1, so the sum leaves 5. Reducing the exponents, or reducing only one term, gives a distractor.

items.question: How many integers p with 30 <= p <= 55 have the property that the units digit of p^4 - p^3 is 0 and p is a multiple of 3?
items.explanation: The units digit of p^4 - p^3 depends only on p mod 10. In the range 30 to 55 there are 11 integers with units digit 0, namely 30, 31, 35, 36, 40, 41, 45, 46, 50, 51, 55. Of those, the multiples of 3 are 30, 36, 45, 51, so the count is 4. Counting only the units-digit condition gives 11, and counting only the multiples of 3 in the range gives 9.

items.question: A panel has 3 members from group A, 6 from group B and 4 from group C. A committee of 6 is to be formed with 1 from A, 3 from B and 2 from C, and the 6 chosen members are to sit in a row of 6 chairs with the leftmost chair always taken by a member of group A. In addition, the members from group C must sit next to each other. In how many ways can this be done?
items.explanation: Choose the members in 3 x 20 x 6 = 360 ways. With the leftmost chair fixed for a member of A, the remaining 5 chairs must hold the other members with the 2 members of C in one block; counting those seatings gives 17280 in all, verified by enumerating every choice of members and every seating. Ignoring the adjacency condition gives 43200, and ignoring the leftmost restriction gives 86400.

items.question: 11 identical balls are to be placed into 9 urns so that no urn is left empty (at least 1 ball in each urn), and the first urn holds exactly 2 balls. In how many ways can this be done?
items.explanation: Fix the first urn at 2 balls, leaving 9 balls for the other 8 urns, each needing at least 1. Give each of them 1, leaving 1 balls to distribute freely among 8 urns, which stars and bars counts as C(8, 7) = 8. With exactly 1 ball in the first urn there would be 36 ways, and ignoring the first-urn condition there are 45.

items.question: How many 5-digit numbers with distinct digits from 1 to 8 are odd and do NOT contain the digit 5?
items.explanation: The units digit must be odd and cannot be 5, so it is 1, 3 or 7 (3 choices). The other four places are filled from the remaining six digits, excluding 5 and the units digit, in P(6,4) = 360 ways. The total is 3 x 360 = 1080. The count was verified by enumerating all arrangements.

items.question: A machine attempts a task repeatedly, succeeding each time with probability 1/2, independently. How few attempts are needed for the probability of at least 2 successes to exceed 0.95?
items.explanation: With n attempts, P(at least 2 successes) = 1 - P(0 or 0 or 1 successes). For n = 8 this is 0.9648, which exceeds 0.95, while for n = 7 it is 0.9375, which does not. A single formula for the mean, or ignoring the complement, gives a distractor.

items.question: A container holds 8 black, 9 white and 4 red balls. Three balls are drawn at random, and two of them turn out to be one black and one white. What is the probability that the third ball is red, and what is the probability that the third ball is white? Give the red probability first, then the white probability.
items.explanation: After the two revealed balls are set aside, 19 balls remain: 7 black, 8 white and 4 red. The third ball is red with probability 4/19, and white with probability 8/19. The two probabilities differ because twice as many white balls as red balls remain. Using the original 21 balls instead of the 19 that remain gives 4/21 and 3/7, and assuming the three colours are equally likely after the reveal gives 1/3 and 1/3.

items.question: Two fair dice are rolled. Given that the sum of the two dice is greater than 10, what is the probability that the first die shows 5, and what is the probability that the first die shows 6? Give the probability for 5 first, then the probability for 6.
items.explanation: The condition leaves only three outcomes: (5, 6), (6, 5) and (6, 6). The first die shows 5 in only one of them, (5, 6), so that probability is 1/3. The first die shows 6 in two of them, (6, 5) and (6, 6), so that probability is 2/3. The two values differ because 6 can pair with two seconds that clear the threshold while 5 can pair with only one. Using the unconditioned 1/6, or swapping the two answers, gives a distractor, and the reversed conditioning gives 1/6 and 1/3.

items.question: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. What is the probability of getting at least 2 heads and at least 1 tail, and what is the probability of getting at least 2 heads given that at least 1 tail appears? Give the first probability first, then the second.
items.explanation: Of the 16 equally likely outcomes, 11 have at least 2 heads, but 1 of those is all heads and has no tail, leaving 10 outcomes with at least 2 heads and at least 1 tail, a probability of 10/16, which is 5/8. Given that at least 1 tail appears, the sample space shrinks to the 15 outcomes that are not all heads, and 10 of those have at least 2 heads, so the conditional probability is 10/15, which is 2/3. Counting only the heads condition gives 11/16, and counting exactly 2 heads gives 3/8.

items.question: There are three urns. Urn A holds 4 black and 1 white balls, urn B holds 2 black and 3 white balls, and urn C holds 2 black and 3 white balls. An urn is chosen, but not equally: urn A is chosen with probability 1/2, urn B with probability 1/3 and urn C with probability 1/6. A ball is drawn from the chosen urn; the ball is black. What is the probability that the ball came from urn A?
items.explanation: By Bayes' rule with unequal choice probabilities, P(A | black) is proportional to (1/2) x 4/5 = 2/5, P(B | black) to (1/3) x 2/5 = 2/15, and P(C | black) to (1/6) x 2/5 = 1/15. The total is 3/5, so P(A | black) = 2/5/3/5 = 2/3. With equal choice probabilities the answer would be 2/3, and P(B | black) here is 2/9.

items.question: In the Units produced (in thousands) by region table, which region showed the largest percentage increase from Q1 to Q4, and which region showed the second-largest percentage increase? Give the largest first, then the second-largest.
